title: Comparing and Ordering Numbers Grade 3 (Up to 10,000) + Free Quiz
meta_title: Comparing and Ordering Numbers Grade 3 + Quiz
meta_desc: Teach comparing and ordering numbers in Grade 3 up to 10,000 with the greater-than sign, the crocodile trick and place value. Free 8-question quiz inside.
excerpt: The crocodile mouth always eats the bigger number — but that trick only works once a child can decide which number is bigger. Here is the place-value method for comparing and ordering numbers up to 10,000, with a quick quiz to test it.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Write 2,463 and 2,436 on a slate and ask a Grade 3 child which is bigger, and you will often get the wrong answer with total confidence. That is the whole challenge with comparing and ordering numbers in Grade 3: once numbers reach four digits, up to 10,000, you cannot just count or eyeball them. You need a method. The good news is the method is short, and there is a trick children genuinely enjoy that makes the symbols stick.

This is not a place-value lesson — a child should already know that in 2,463 the 2 means two thousands and the 4 means four hundreds. What we are doing here is putting that knowledge to work to decide which of two numbers is larger, and then to line up a whole set of them in order.

The three symbols: >, < and =

Grade 3 is where the greater-than sign, less-than sign and equals sign stop being decoration and start doing real work. Here is the plain meaning:

  • > means ‘is greater than’. So 5,200 > 3,900 reads ‘5,200 is greater than 3,900’.
  • < means ‘is less than’. So 480 < 4,800 reads ‘480 is less than 4,800’.
  • = means ‘is equal to’. Both sides are exactly the same, like 1,000 = 1,000.

The hungry crocodile mouth

The classic trick, and the one I still reach for first: the symbol is a hungry crocodile’s mouth, and the crocodile always wants to eat the bigger number. So the wide open end faces the larger number and the pointy end faces the smaller one. For 7,000 and 900, the mouth opens towards 7,000: 7,000 > 900. Children remember ‘the mouth eats the bigger number’ long after they forget which name goes with which symbol.

One honest caveat. The crocodile is a memory aid for writing the symbol correctly — it does not tell you which number is actually bigger. For that, you still need the place-value method below. I have seen children draw a lovely crocodile and still point it the wrong way because they never worked out which number was larger first.

The place-value method: compare the highest place first

This is the real skill. To compare two whole numbers, line them up by place value and start from the left — the highest place — not the right. Compare digit by digit until the digits differ; the first place where they differ decides it.

Take 4,271 and 4,208. Both are four-digit numbers, so compare thousands: 4 and 4, tied. Compare hundreds: 2 and 2, tied. Compare tens: 7 and 0 — and there it is. 7 tens beats 0 tens, so 4,271 > 4,208. You never even look at the ones. The moment one digit wins, the comparison is over.

Count the digits first

Before comparing digit by digit, there is a faster shortcut for many pairs: count how many digits each number has. A number with more digits is always bigger (for whole numbers with no leading zeros). 980 has three digits; 1,004 has four; so 1,004 is the larger one without comparing a single digit. This is the step children skip most often, and it is the one that would have saved the child at the top of this article.

CompareFirst place that differsResult
980 and 1,004Different digit counts (3 vs 4)980 < 1,004
5,600 and 5,060Hundreds: 6 beats 05,600 > 5,060
3,333 and 3,330Ones: 3 beats 03,333 > 3,330
7,102 and 7,102No digit differs7,102 = 7,102

Ordering a set: ascending and descending

Once a child can compare two numbers, ordering a whole set is just comparing repeatedly. Two words to get right, because exams use them: ascending means smallest to largest (going up, like climbing stairs), and descending means largest to smallest (going down).

Here is the routine I teach for ordering. Take the set 3,412; 3,240; 812; 3,410.

  • Group by digit count. 812 has three digits, so it is the smallest — set it aside as first.
  • Compare the rest place by place. Among 3,412; 3,240; 3,410, the thousands all tie at 3. Hundreds: 4, 2, 4. So 3,240 is smallest of these.
  • Break the remaining tie. 3,412 and 3,410 both have 3,4 at the front; the tens tie at 1; the ones decide: 2 beats 0.

Ascending order: 812, 3,240, 3,410, 3,412. For descending, simply reverse it: 3,412, 3,410, 3,240, 812. Finding the smallest and the largest is the same job — the smallest is the first in ascending order, the largest is the last.

The mistakes to watch for

Three errors come up again and again with Grade 3, and knowing them in advance saves a lot of red ink.

  • Comparing from the right. A child compares the ones first and decides 4,208 > 4,271 because 8 > 1. Always start from the left.
  • Longer looks bigger. A number that looks long on the page is not always larger — but with whole numbers and no leading zeros, more digits genuinely does mean bigger, so teach the digit-count check properly rather than by vague guessing.
  • Pointing the crocodile by habit. Some children always open the mouth to the left. Decide which number is bigger first, then draw the symbol.

Try the quiz, then the worksheet

Below is a free eight-question quiz on comparing and ordering numbers up to 10,000 — the symbols, the place-value method, and putting a set in order. Let your child work through it and read each explanation for anything they miss. When they are ready for longer written practice, the printable worksheet at the end has graded questions with a full answer key.

questions.q: What is the smallest number in this set: 2,700; 2,070; 2,007; 2,077 ?
questions.explanation: Thousands all tie at 2. Hundreds: 7, 0, 0, 0 — so 2,700 is largest, not smallest. Among the rest the tens decide: 2,007 has 0 tens and 0 ones, making it the smallest.
Compare hundreds: 3,500 has 5 hundreds, 3,050 has 0 hundreds. So 3,500 is greater: 3,500 > 3,050.
Descending means largest first. 615 has three digits, so it is smallest and goes last. Between 6,150 and 6,015 the hundreds are 1 and 0, so 6,150 is largest. Descending: 6,150; 6,015; 615.

faq.q: What does comparing and ordering numbers mean in Grade 3?
faq.a: Comparing means deciding whether one number is greater than, less than or equal to another using the >, < and = signs. Ordering means arranging a set of numbers from smallest to largest (ascending) or largest to smallest (descending). In Grade 3 this is done with numbers up to 10,000.

faq.q: How do you compare two four-digit numbers?
faq.a: First count the digits — more digits means a bigger number. If both have the same number of digits, compare from the left, one place at a time, starting with the thousands. The first place where the digits differ decides which number is larger; you can stop there.

faq.q: What is the crocodile trick for the greater-than and less-than signs?
faq.a: Picture the symbol as a hungry crocodile’s mouth that always wants to eat the bigger number. The wide open end faces the larger number and the pointy end faces the smaller one. It helps a child write the symbol the right way round, but they must still work out which number is bigger first.

faq.q: What is the difference between ascending and descending order?
faq.a: Ascending order goes from smallest to largest, like climbing stairs upward. Descending order goes from largest to smallest. Once a set is arranged one way, you can simply reverse it to get the other order.
